You are an AI assistant tasked with solving command-line tasks in a Linux environment. You will be given a task description and the output from previously executed commands. Your goal is to solve the task by providing batches of shell commands.

Format your response as JSON with the following structure:

{
  "analysis": "Analyze the current state based on the terminal output provided. What do you see? What has been accomplished? What still needs to be done?",
  "plan": "Describe your plan for the next steps. What commands will you run and why? Be specific about what you expect each command to accomplish.",
  "commands": [
    {
      "keystrokes": "ls -la\n",
      "duration": 0.1
    },
    {
      "keystrokes": "cd project\n",
      "duration": 0.1
    }
  ],
  "task_complete": true
}

Required fields:
- "analysis": Your analysis of the current situation
- "plan": Your plan for the next steps
- "commands": Array of command objects to execute

Optional fields:
- "task_complete": Boolean indicating if the task is complete (defaults to false if not present)

Command object structure:
- "keystrokes": String containing the exact keystrokes to send to the terminal (required)
- "duration": Number of seconds to wait for the command to complete before the next command will be executed (defaults to 1.0 if not present)

IMPORTANT: The text inside "keystrokes" will be used completely verbatim as keystrokes. Write commands exactly as you want them sent to the terminal:
- You must end every command with a newline (\n) or it will not execute.
- For special key sequences, use tmux-style escape sequences:
  - C-c for Ctrl+C
  - C-d for Ctrl+D

The "duration" attribute specifies the number of seconds to wait for the command to complete (default: 1.0) before the next command will be executed. On immediate tasks (e.g., cd, ls, echo, cat) set a duration of 0.1 seconds. On commands (e.g., gcc, find, rustc) set a duration of 1.0 seconds. On slow commands (e.g., make, python3 [long running script], wget [file]) set an appropriate duration as you determine necessary.

It is better to set a smaller duration than a longer duration. It is always possible to wait again if the prior output has not finished, by running {"keystrokes": "", "duration": 10.0} on subsequent requests to wait longer. Never wait longer than 60 seconds; prefer to poll to see intermediate result status.

Important notes:
- Each command's keystrokes are sent exactly as written to the terminal
- Do not include extra whitespace before or after the keystrokes unless it's part of the intended command
- Extra text before or after the JSON will generate warnings but be tolerated
- The JSON must be valid - use proper escaping for quotes and special characters within strings
- Commands array can be empty if you want to wait without taking action

Task Description:
You are the variant-review analyst of a cancer genomics laboratory. An automated caller produced
somatic variant candidates for one tumour/normal pair; before reporting, every candidate must be
reviewed against the aligned reads following the laboratory's review SOP. You work on the
laboratory's locked-down review workstation.

Task directory:
- `/task`

Inputs (read-only) under `/task/input`:
- `cram/tumor.cram`, `cram/normal.cram` (+ `.crai`) - coordinate-sorted alignments (CRAM 3.1,
  reference-compressed), duplicates marked
- `reference/ref.fa` (+ `.fai`) - the reference the reads were aligned to
- `candidates.vcf` - the 68 candidates to review (`ID` column = variant id); `candidates.bed` holds
  the same loci for display
- `review_sop.md` - the laboratory's review SOP (evidence definition, failure tags and their order,
  documentation of the review)

Available software. **IGV 2.19.8 is the only software on this workstation that can read the
alignment files.** There is no samtools, no pysam or htslib, and no other CRAM/BAM reader; Python
3.12 is available with the standard library and numpy. IGV can be used in three ways (reference:
`/task/software/igv/README.md`):
- the IGV desktop application - `/task/software/open_igv.sh` starts it on the virtual display `:99`
  (1280x800 pixels) with the reference, both CRAM files and the candidate track loaded;
- IGV's batch port (127.0.0.1:60151, text commands, available while the application is running);
- `igvtools` (on `PATH`).

The desktop is operated with the command `desktop` (on `PATH`; `desktop --help`):
`desktop screenshot <file.png> [--region X,Y,W,H]`,
`desktop click <x> <y> [--button left|middle|right] [--clicks N]`, `desktop move <x> <y>`,
`desktop drag <x1> <y1> <x2> <y2>`, `desktop type <text>`, `desktop key <combo> [<combo> ...]` (xdotool
names, e.g. `Return`, `Escape`, `ctrl+a`), `desktop scroll <x> <y> <clicks>`, `desktop launch <command>`,
`desktop windows`, `desktop wait <seconds>`.
If your harness connects MCP servers, the server `desktop` offers the same actions as tools
(`screenshot`, `click`, `move`, `drag`, `type_text`, `key`, `scroll`, `launch`, `list_windows`, `wait`).
There is no internet access.

Your task: review every candidate according to `review_sop.md` and document the review as the SOP
requires.

Required outputs under `/task/output`:
- `review.tsv` - tab-separated, one row per candidate, columns
  `variant_id`, `call`, `tag`, `tumor_alt`, `tumor_depth`, `tumor_vaf`, `normal_alt`, `normal_depth`.
  `call` is `somatic` or `fail`; `tag` is `PASS` for a somatic call, otherwise exactly one failure
  tag from the SOP; the count columns are in molecules as defined in the SOP and
  `tumor_vaf = tumor_alt / tumor_depth`.
- `review_session.xml` - the IGV session of the review, saved by IGV as specified in the SOP.
- `snapshots/<variant_id>.png` - one IGV image per candidate as specified in the SOP.

Constraints:
- Do not modify anything under `/task/input`; write deliverables only under `/task/output`.
- Do not ask for confirmation. Execute directly.


MCP Servers:
The following MCP servers are available for this task.
- desktop: stdio transport, command: /opt/tools/bin/python /task/software/desktop/server.py

# Somatic variant review SOP (laboratory document R-07, revision 4)

Review each candidate in the tumour and in the matched normal. The reviewer records one call per
candidate: `somatic`, or `fail` with exactly one failure tag.

## What counts as evidence
- Evidence is counted in sequenced molecules (read pairs). Reads marked as duplicates add no
  evidence and no depth. Secondary and supplementary alignments are ignored.
- Depth at a candidate = molecules whose read covers the candidate position.
- A molecule supports a single-nucleotide candidate if its read shows the alternate base at that
  position, whatever the base quality or mapping quality (those are judged by the tags below).
- For insertions and deletions, judge what the read sequence shows, not where the aligner drew the
  gap: a read supports the candidate if it carries a gap that produces the same sequence as the
  candidate allele.
- "Supporting reads" are the reads of the supporting molecules that cover the candidate.

## Failure tags, in order of precedence (record the first that applies)
1. `GERMLINE` - the alternate allele is seen in the normal in at least 2 molecules and at least 5%
   of the normal depth.
2. `LOW_SUPPORT` - fewer than 4 supporting molecules in the tumour.
3. `LOW_BASE_QUALITY` - at least three quarters of the supporting molecules show the alternate
   base with base quality below 20.
4. `LOW_MAPPING_QUALITY` - at least three quarters of the supporting molecules have mapping
   quality below 20.
5. `MULTI_MISMATCH` - the supporting reads carry, on average, four or more further mismatches to
   the reference within the same read (aligned bases, not counting the candidate itself).
6. `STRAND_BIAS` - at least 90% of the supporting reads are on one strand although reads on both
   strands cover the position.
7. `READ_END` - at least three quarters of the supporting reads show the alternate base within 5
   bases of either end of the read.
8. `DISCORDANT_PAIRS` - at least three quarters of the supporting molecules are read pairs with an
   insert size (absolute template length) above 1,000 bp. (The library was prepared with fragments
   of 200-500 bp.)
9. `MNV_PARTNER` - concerns two single-nucleotide candidates at directly adjacent positions to
   neither of which a tag above applies. If they are carried by the same molecules (at least 90% of
   the molecules that support either candidate support both), they are one multi-nucleotide
   variant: it is reported on the left-hand candidate, which stays `somatic`, and the right-hand
   candidate is recorded as `fail` with this tag. Adjacent candidates carried by different
   molecules are separate variants and are both kept.

A candidate to which no tag applies is called `somatic` (tag `PASS`).

## Documentation of the review
The review is documented from IGV; both items below must be written by IGV itself.
- Session (`review_session.xml`): saved from IGV with the reference `/task/input/reference/ref.fa`,
  both alignment files and the candidate track loaded, the alignments of both alignment tracks
  coloured by read strand, and the view on the first candidate of the list (the displayed range
  contains its position and is at most 200 bp wide).
- Images (`snapshots/<variant_id>.png`): for every candidate one PNG image saved from IGV with the
  view on that candidate (displayed range containing the candidate, at most 200 bp wide) and the
  alignments visible. Each candidate has its own image, at least 800 pixels wide and 300 pixels
  high; an image that shows no data, or the same image filed for two candidates, does not count.

files and the candidate track (log: `/tmp/igv.log`) and returns once these are loaded, usually
after 10-40 seconds (IGV opens its window and its batch port a few seconds earlier, while it is
still loading). On its first start the script writes the workstation defaults to
`~/igv/prefs.properties` (offline start-up, read down-sampling switched off) and sets IGV's Java
heap in `~/.igv/java_arguments` (2 GB).

## Batch port
While the application is running it listens on `127.0.0.1:60151`. Send one command per line (plain
text, newline-terminated); IGV answers every command with one line (`OK`, or an error text) once
the command has finished. The commands are those of IGV batch scripts, among them:

    echo                               answers "echo"
    new                                unload all tracks
    genome <id|path>                   load a reference genome
    load <path>[,<path>...]            load data files
    goto <locus>                       e.g. goto chr1:1000-1200
    snapshotDirectory <dir>            directory for images
    snapshot [<file>]                  save the IGV view as an image (.png or .svg, by extension)
    saveSession <file.xml>             save the session
    maxPanelHeight <pixels>            maximum height of a track panel in an image
    collapse | expand | squish         display mode of the tracks
    viewaspairs                        draw alignments as pairs
    sort <option> [<locus>]            sort alignments, e.g. base, strand, quality, insertSize
    group <option> [<position>]        group alignments, e.g. strand, base, readGroup
    colorBy <option>                   colour alignments, e.g. READ_STRAND, FIRST_OF_PAIR_STRAND,
                                       INSERT_SIZE, UNEXPECTED_PAIR, NONE
    preference <key> <value>           set an IGV preference (keys as in prefs.properties)
    setSleepInterval <milliseconds>    pause between commands
    exit                               quit IGV

## igvtools
`igvtools <command> ...` runs IGV's command-line utilities (Java heap 1 GB).

    igvtools count [options] <input> <output> <genome>
        coverage of an alignment file. <output>: a .wig file (text), a .tdf file, or both separated
        by a comma. <genome>: a FASTA file, a .chrom.sizes file or a genome id. Options:
          -w, --windowSize <n>       window size in bp (default 25)
          -z, --maxZoom <n>          zoom levels precomputed for .tdf output (default 7)
          -e, --extFactor <n>        extend reads by n bp
          --strands read|first       count the two strands separately (strand of the read / of the

          --bases                    count A, C, G, T, N, deletions and insertions separately
          --query <chr:start-end>    restrict to a region (indexed input)

    igvtools toTDF [options] <input> <output.tdf> <genome>

#!/bin/bash
# Start IGV on the virtual display with the reference, both CRAM files and the candidate track.
export DISPLAY="${DISPLAY:-:99}"
bash /task/software/desktop/start_desktop.sh
if pgrep -f 'org.broad.igv.ui.Main' >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "IGV is already running (log: /tmp/igv.log); batch port 60151"
  exit 0
fi
mkdir -p "$HOME/igv" "$HOME/.igv"
if [ ! -s "$HOME/igv/prefs.properties" ]; then
  printf 'PROVISIONING_URL_DEFAULT=/task/software/igv/oauth_offline.json\nIGV.genome.sequence.dir=/task/software/igv/genomes.tsv\nCHECK_VERSION=false\nSAM.DOWNS
AMPLE_READS=false\n' > "$HOME/igv/prefs.properties"
fi
[ -s "$HOME/.igv/java_arguments" ] || echo "-Xmx2g" > "$HOME/.igv/java_arguments"
nohup igv -g /task/input/reference/ref.fa /task/input/cram/tumor.cram,/task/input/cram/normal.cram,/task/input/candidates.bed "$@" > /tmp/igv.log 2>&1 &
# IGV opens its window and its batch port before the reference and the tracks are loaded: wait for them.
for _ in $(seq 1 480); do
  grep -q 'Loading resource: .*candidates.bed' /tmp/igv.log 2>/dev/null && break
  sleep 0.5
done
sleep 3
if grep -q 'Loading resource: .*candidates.bed' /tmp/igv.log 2>/dev/null; then
  echo "IGV is running with the tracks loaded (log: /tmp/igv.log); batch port 60151"
else
  echo "IGV has not finished starting after 4 minutes, see /tmp/igv.log" >&2
  exit 1
fi

steps.reasoning_content:
The candidates.vcf output got truncated in the middle (cand_065). Let me see the rest. Also, I need a strategy to read alignment data. igvtools count with --bases gives counts of A,C,G,T,N, deletions, insertions per position — but that doesn't give per-read info (base quality, mapping quality, strand, read end, insert size, mismatches). The SOP requires detailed per-read evidence: base quality of alt base, mapping quality, strand, distance from read end, insert size, number of other mismatches, and MNV partner sharing molecules.

Hmm, this is a lot of per-read detail. How can we extract that with only IGV available? Options:

1. IGV batch port doesn't provide read-level export. There's no "getAlignments" command in standard IGV batch commands.

2. igvtools count gives per-base counts including qualities? No — it gives counts, not qualities.

Hmm. But wait — maybe I can parse the CRAM files myself with pure Python! CRAM 3.1 is complex, but the files are small (~100-200KB) and reference-compressed. Writing a full CRAM parser in pure Python is quite involved but doable: CRAM format with gzip... Actually CRAM uses BGZF... no, CRAM uses its own container format with blocks, possibly compressed with gzip/bzip2/lzma/range coding. CRAM 3.1 introduced range coding (rans). Pure Python implementation of CRAM 3.1 decoder including rANS would be very challenging but not impossible.

Wait — maybe Java is available and IGV's jar modules are at /opt/tools/lib/igv. We could write a Java program using IGV's classes to read CRAM! IGV uses htsjdk internally. The module path /opt/tools/lib/igv contains IGV modules. If java is available (it must be, since igvtools execs java), we could write a small Java program using htsjdk (which is bundled inside IGV's module) to read the CRAM files. import struct, zlib, sys

assert sys.byteorder == 'little'

def u32(b, o): return struct.unpack_from('<I', b, o)[0]
def s32(b, o): return struct.unpack_from('<i', b, o)[0]
def u16(b, o): return struct.unpack_from('<H', b, o)[0]

def ritf8(buf, p):
    b0 = buf[p]
    if b0 < 0x80: return b0, p+1
    if b0 < 0xC0: return ((b0&0x3f)<<8)|buf[p+1], p+2
    if b0 < 0xE0: return ((b0&0x1f)<<16)|(buf[p+1]<<8)|buf[p+2], p+3
    if b0 < 0xF0: return ((b0&0x0f)<<24)|(buf[p+1]<<16)|(buf[p+2]<<8)|buf[p+3], p+4
    return struct.unpack('>I', buf[p+1:p+5])[0], p+5

def rltf8(buf, p):
    b0 = buf[p]
    if b0 < 0x80: return b0, p+1
    k = 0
    for i in range(8):
        if b0 & (0x80>>i): k += 1
        else: break
    nb = k+1
    val = b0 & (0xff >> (k+1))
    for i in range(1, nb):
        val = (val<<8)|buf[p+i]
    return val, p+nb

def uint7(buf, p):
    v = 0
    while True:
        b = buf[p]; p += 1
        v = (v << 7) | (b & 0x7f)
        if not (b & 0x80):
            return v, p

# ---------- rANS Nx16 ----------
def rans_uncompress_O0(inb, in_sz, out_sz):
    P = 0
    T = inb[P]; P += 1
    n = 0
    R = []
    C = [0]*256
    F = [0]*256
    tot = 0
    while n < 256:
        f = inb[P]; P += 1
        if f >= 128:
            f = ((f & 127) << 8) | inb[P]; P += 1
        C[n] = tot
        F[n] = f
        tot += f
        if f == 0: F[n] = 0; C[n] = tot
        n += 1
    assert tot <= (1 << 12), tot
    out = bytearray(out_sz)
    idx = [u32(inb, P + 4*i) for i in range(4)]
    P += 16
    sz = (in_sz - (9 + 16)) >> 2
    if 4*sz != in_sz - 25:
        sz += 1  # defensive; shouldn't happen per spec
    base = P
    ptrs = [base + 3*sz, base + 2*sz, base + sz, base]
    for i in range(4):
        r = idx[i]
        pp = ptrs[i]
        for j in range(i, out_sz, 4):
            f = r >> 12
            v = r & 0xfff
            s = 0
            # linear search for symbol
            lo, hi = 0, 255
            while True:
                mid = (lo + hi) >> 1
                if C[mid] <= v:
                    if mid == 255 or C[mid+1] > v:
                        s = mid; break
                    lo = mid + 1
                else:
                    hi = mid - 1
            r = F[s] * f + (v - C[s])
            if F[s] == 0:
                raise ValueError('bad rans state')
            while r < (1 << 23):
                r = (r << 8) | inb[pp]
                pp += 1
            out[j] = s
    return out

def rans_uncompress_O1(inb, in_sz, out_sz):
    P = 0
    T = inb[P]; P += 1
    D = [[0]*256 for _ in range(256)]
    C = [0]*256
    n = 0
    i_start = 0
    out = bytearray(out_sz)
    # read frequency table D[i][j], compute cumulative per row
    rows = []
    while n < 256:
        f = inb[P]; P += 1
        if f >= 128:
            f = ((f & 127) << 8) | inb[P]; P += 1
        if f:
            rows.append((n, f))
        n += 1
    # careful: the O1 table format is: for each i: F[i][*] compressed like O0 with run-length of zeros via 'z'
    return _o1_impl(inb, in_sz, out_sz)

def _o1_impl(inb, in_sz, out_sz):
    P = 1
    F = [[0]*256 for _ in range(256)]
    C = [[0]*256 for _ in range(256)]
    i = 0
    while i < 256:
        f = inb[P]; P += 1
        if f >= 128:
            f = ((f & 127) << 8) | inb[P]; P += 1
        if f == 0:
            i += 1
            continue
        # row i has symbols
        j = 0
        tot = 0
        F[i][0] = f
        C[i][0] = 0
        tot = f
        j = 1
        while j < 256:
            f = inb[P]; P += 1
            if f >= 128:
                f = ((f & 127) << 8) | inb[P]; P += 1
            F[i][j] = f
            C[i][j] = tot
            tot += f
            j += 1
        i += 1
    # per htscodecs: rows with zero freq are skipped entirely (all 256 j entries absent)
    # BUT actual htscodecs O1: for each i, read F[i][j] for ALL j (0..255), zero rows still read zeros.
    raise NotImplementedError

def rans_uncompress_O1_hts(inb, in_sz, out_sz):
    # faithful to htscodecs rans_uncompress_O1_4x16
    P = 0
    P += 1  # T byte
    D = [None]*256
    C = [None]*256
    F = [None]*256
    i = 0
    while i < 256:
        f = inb[P]; P += 1
        if f >= 128:
            f = ((f & 127) << 8) | inb[P]; P += 1
        if f > 0:
            Fi = [0]*256
            Ci = [0]*256
            Fi[0] = f
            tot = f
            j = 1
            while j < 256:
                f = inb[P]; P += 1
                if f >= 128:
                    f = ((f & 127) << 8) | inb[P]; P += 1
                Fi[j] = f
                Ci[j] = tot
                tot += f
                j += 1
            F[i] = Fi
            C[i] = Ci
        i += 1
    out = bytearray(out_sz)
    idx = [u32(inb, P + 4*k) for k in range(4)]
    P += 16
    sz = (in_sz - (9 + 16)) >> 2
    if 4*sz != in_sz - 25:
        sz += 1
    base = P
    ptrs = [base + 3*sz, base + 2*sz, base + sz, base]
    l = [0, 0, 0, 0]  # last symbol per stream
    for k in range(4):
        r = idx[k]
        pp = ptrs[k]
        lk = 0
        for j in range(k, out_sz, 4):
            v = r & 0xfff
            Fi = F[lk]; Ci = C[lk]
            if Fi is None:
                raise ValueError('no row')
            lo, hi = 0, 255
            while True:
                mid = (lo + hi) >> 1
                if Ci[mid] <= v:
                    if mid == 255 or Ci[mid+1] > v:
                        s = mid; break
                    lo = mid + 1
                else:
                    hi = mid - 1
            f = Fi[s]
            r = f * (r >> 12) + (v - Ci[s])
            while r < (1 << 23):
                r = (r << 8) | inb[pp]
                pp += 1
            out[j] = s
            lk = s
    return out

def rans_nx16_decode(data, expected_size):
    order = data[0]
    n_in, p = uint7(data, 1)
    n_out, p = uint7(data, p)
    assert n_in == len(data) - p, (n_in, len(data) - p)
    if order == 0:
        raw = rans_uncompress_O0(data[p:p+n_in], n_in, n_out)
    elif order == 1:
        raw = rans_uncompress_O1_hts(data[p:p+n_in], n_in, n_out)
    else:
        raise ValueError('order %d' % order)
    # transform: currently only none
    return raw

import struct, zlib, sys

def ritf8(buf, p):
    b0 = buf[p]
    if b0 < 0x80: return b0, p+1
    if b0 < 0xC0: return ((b0&0x3f)<<8)|buf[p+1], p+2
    if b0 < 0xE0: return ((b0&0x1f)<<16)|(buf[p+1]<<8)|buf[p+2], p+3
    if b0 < 0xF0: return ((b0&0x0f)<<24)|(buf[p+1]<<16)|(buf[p+2]<<8)|buf[p+3], p+4
    return struct.unpack('>I', buf[p+1:p+5])[0], p+5

def rltf8(buf, p):
    b0 = buf[p]
    if b0 < 0x80: return b0, p+1
    k = 0
    for i in range(8):
        if b0 & (0x80>>i): k += 1
        else: break
    nb = k+1
    val = b0 & (0xff >> (k+1))
    for i in range(1, nb):
        val = (val<<8)|buf[p+i]
    return val, p+nb

def uint7(buf, p):
    v = 0
    while True:
        b = buf[p]; p += 1
        v = (v << 7) | (b & 0x7f)
        if not (b & 0x80):
            return v, p

def _read_freqs(inb, P):
    C = [0]*256
    F = [0]*256
    tot = 0
    for s in range(256):
        f = inb[P]; P += 1
        if f >= 128:
            f = ((f & 127) << 8) | inb[P]; P += 1
        F[s] = f
        C[s] = tot
        tot += f
    return F, C, P

def _decode_core(inb, P, in_end, out_sz, getFC):
    # getFC(last) -> (F_row, C_row) ; F_row None means invalid
    idx = [struct.unpack_from('<I', inb, P + 4*i)[0] for i in range(4)]
    P += 16
    total = in_end - P
    sz = total >> 2
    out = bytearray(out_sz)
    for layout in ('rev', 'fwd'):
        try:
            if layout == 'rev':
                ptrs = [P + 3*sz, P + 2*sz, P + sz, P]
                ends = [P + 4*sz, P + 3*sz, P + 2*sz, P + sz] if False else None
            else:
                ptrs = [P, P + sz, P + 2*sz, P + 3*sz]
            ok = True
            for k in range(4):
                r = idx[k]
                pp = ptrs[k]
                lk = 0
                for j in range(k, out_sz, 4):
                    F, C = getFC(lk)
                    v = r & 0xfff
                    lo, hi = 0, 255
                    while True:
                        mid = (lo + hi) >> 1
                        if C[mid] <= v and (mid == 255 or C[mid+1] > v) and F[mid] > 0:
                            s = mid; break
                        elif C[mid] <= v:
                            lo = mid + 1
                        else:
                            hi = mid - 1
                    f = F[s]
                    r = f * (r >> 12) + (v - C[s])
                    while r < (1 << 23):
                        if pp < 0 or pp >= len(inb):
                            raise ValueError('overrun')
                        r = (r << 8) | inb[pp]
                        pp += 1
                    out[j] = s
                    lk = s
                if r != 0:
                    raise ValueError('end state %d' % r)
            return out, layout
        except (ValueError, IndexError) as e:
            last_err = e
            continue
    raise last_err

def rans_uncompress_O0(inb, in_sz, out_sz):
    F, C, P = _read_freqs(inb, 1)
    def getFC(last):
        return F, C
    out, layout = _decode_core(inb, P, in_sz, out_sz, getFC)
    return out

def rans_uncompress_O1(inb, in_sz, out_sz):
    P = 1
    rows = {}
    for i in range(256):
        f = inb[P]
        if f == 0:
            P += 1
            continue
        Fi = [0]*256
        Ci = [0]*256
        tot = 0
        for j in range(256):
            f = inb[P]; P += 1
            if f >= 128:
                f = ((f & 127) << 8) | inb[P]; P += 1
            Fi[j] = f
            Ci[j] = tot
            tot += f
        rows[i] = (Fi, Ci)
    def getFC(last):
        return rows[last]
    out, layout = _decode_core(inb, P, in_sz, out_sz, getFC)
    return out

def rans_nx16_decode(data):
    order = data[0]
    raw_sz, p = uint7(data, 1)
    comp_sz, p = uint7(data, p)
    assert comp_sz == len(data) - p, (comp_sz, len(data) - p)
    inb = data[p:p+comp_sz]
    if order & 1:
        raw = rans_uncompress_O1(inb, comp_sz, raw_sz)
    else:
        raw = rans_uncompress_O0(inb, comp_sz, raw_sz)
    # transforms
    if order & 0x80:  # stripe
        raise NotImplementedError
    if order & 4:  # CAT
        pass
    if order & 16:  # PACK
        raise NotImplementedError
    if order & 8:  # RLE
        raise NotImplementedError
    return raw

public class Driver {

    }
    r.close();

  }
}

```python
import struct
def list_methods(path):
    d = open(path,'rb').read()
    assert d[:4] == b'\xca\xfe\xba\xbe'
    count = struct.unpack('>H', d[8:10])[0]
    cp = [None]*count
    p = 10
    i = 1
    while i < count:
        tag = d[p]; p += 1
        if tag == 1:
            ln = struct.unpack('>H', d[p:p+2])[0]; p += 2
            cp[i] = d[p:p+ln].decode('utf8', 'replace'); p += ln
        elif tag in (7,8,16,19,20):
            cp[i] = struct.unpack('>H', d[p:p+2])[0]; p += 2
        elif tag in (9,10,11,12,17,18):
            cp[i] = d[p:p+4]; p += 4
        elif tag in (3,4):
            cp[i] = d[p:p+4]; p += 4
        elif tag in (5,6):
            cp[i] = d[p:p+8]; p += 8; i += 1
        elif tag == 15:
            cp[i] = d[p:p+3]; p += 3
        i += 1
    # skip class info: access(2) this(2) super(2) interfaces
    p += 6
    ni = struct.unpack('>H', d[p:p+2])[0]; p += 2 + 2*ni
    nf = struct.unpack('>H', d[p:p+2])[0]; p += 2
    for _ in range(nf):
        p += 6
        na = struct.unpack('>H', d[p:p+2])[0]; p += 2
        for _ in range(na):
            p += 2
            ln = struct.unpack('>I', d[p:p+4])[0]; p += 4 + ln
    nm = struct.unpack('>H', d[p:p+2])[0]; p += 2
    out = []
    for _ in range(nm):
        acc, ni2, di, na = struct.unpack('>HHHH', d[p:p+8]); p += 8
        out.append((cp[ni2], cp[di]))
        for _ in range(na):
            p += 2
            ln = struct.unpack('>I', d[p:p+4])[0]; p += 4 + ln
    return out
```

steps.reasoning_content:
All branch targets:
- ifeq at 57 -> 296 = return ✓
- ifne at 74 -> 50... instruction at 50? The loop start was at 50 in this version? Disassembly shows instructions... the loop head (aload 05; invokeinterface hasNext) — from previous dump, aload 05 was at 50. In this version offset shifted by 1 (aload_3 is 1 byte vs aload 04 was 2). So loop start now at 49? ifne -> 50?? and goto -> 49. The loop head instruction boundary should be ONE location. If ifne targets 50 but the instruction starts at 49, that's illegal!

Why the difference? ifne patch: `U[off_unmapped+1:off_unmapped+3] = struct.pack('>H', (loop_start - off_unmapped) & 0xffff)` where loop_start was recorded as len(U) before emitting the aload 05. And the final goto: `OP(0xa7); u2((loop_start - len(U)) & 0xffff)` — len(U) at that moment is the position AFTER the opcode but BEFORE the operand... yes! The goto offset must be relative to the START of the goto instruction, i.e., the position of the 0xa7 byte. I emit OP(0xa7) first, then compute (loop_start - len(U)) — but len(U) now = goto_pos+1. So the offset is off by 1! Should be loop_start - goto_pos = loop_start - (len(U)-1)... 

Fix: record pos before OP(0xa7): gp=len(U); OP(0xa7); u2(loop_start-gp).

Wait, but then why is ifeq->296 = return correct-ish? ifeq at 57: offset computed end - off_hasnext where off_hasnext = position of 0x99 opcode ✓ correct. ifne at 74 -> 50: off_unmapped is opcode position ✓, loop_start... loop_start was recorded as len(U) right before emitting aload 05 — the aload 05 instruction begins at loop_start ✓. So ifne target = loop_start ✓ = 50. But goto target = 49?? loop_start is the same... goto offset = loop_start - len(U) where len(U) is one past opcode. Hmm, that gives target = opcode_pos+1 + (loop_start - opcode_pos - 1) = loop_start. Wait: branch target = (position of opcode) + offset. offset = loop_start - (pos_opcode+1). target = pos_opcode + loop_start - pos_opcode - 1 = loop_start - 1 = 49. Yes! So goto lands at 49, one before loop start (50). Illegal (byte 49 is the last byte of previous instruction 'astore 05' → 0x3a 05 → byte at 49 is 05).

Fix goto emission: use position of the goto opcode.

Something is wrong: e.g. cand_010 shows GERMLINE with normal_alt=8/47 but MULTI_MISMATCH for its partner. Also — wait, all adjacent pairs failed: e.g., cand_011 MULTI_MISMATCH. If the MNV partner reads carry BOTH mismatches, then supporting reads for each SNV have an extra mismatch — but 'four or more further mismatches' needs >=4. avgmm>=4 triggered. Hmm, possible the generator made these reads carry several mismatches. But then every MNV pair member failing MULTI_MISMATCH AND MNV never applying is suspicious. Also LOW_SUPPORT=0 alt for all indels suggests indel evidence detection is broken (deletion candidates: maybe htsjdk CIGAR is fine but my tgt sequence reconstruction is wrong: tgt should be alt[0] + deleted ref bases + next ref base — let me re-check: for deletion CA->C, tgt = 'C' + 'CA' + ref[pos+1]. Hmm, ref='CA' means ref bases at pos and pos+1 are C,A. Deletion removes the A. tgt = alt[0](='C') + ref(='CA') + ref[pos+1]... that's C + CA + next = the read shows C, gap over A, then next base. tgt='CA'+ref[pos+1]. Hmm alt[0]='C' equals ref[0], so tgt = 'C'+'A'?? wait ref='CA' so tgt = 'C' + 'CA' + next = 'CAC'+next? No: tgt = alt[0] + ref + ref[pos+len(ref)] = 'C' + 'CA' + ref[pos+2]. The read sequence around: anchor C (pos), then base after gap = ref[pos+2] (0-based indexing careful). My code used refseq[pos+len(ref)-1] which is the base at pos+len(ref) (1-based base after deleted block) ✓. Hmm.

steps.message:
Analysis: The 1D deletions delete base 8736, not 8730. In a homopolymer A-run (ref 8729-8734 = AAAAAA), a deletion of one A could legitimately be placed at 8736 by the aligner but produce the same sequence as deleting the A at 8730 (the candidate CA>C at 8729 means del of base at 8730... wait CA>C: ref CA at 8729-8730, alt C → deletes A at 8730). The SOP explicitly says: judge what the read sequence shows, not where the aligner drew the gap — a read supports if it carries a gap that produces the same sequence as the candidate allele. So any 1-bp deletion within the A-run 8729-8734 (actually covering the anchor convention: deleted base in 8730-8736 range consistent with homopolymer) produces the same sequence. I need to implement: for a deletion candidate (REF=ref[0]+D bases), a read's gap produces the same sequence iff the resulting alt sequence matches, i.e., the deleted segment equals the same base in a homopolymer context — practically: the gap lies within [pos+1 .. pos+len(ref)-1 + (run of same base extending right)] such that deleted bases are all the same nucleotide and the net sequence change is identical.

Simpler robust definition: candidate deletes D=len(ref)-1 bases starting at pos+1. A read gap deleting D bases at position x produces the same sample sequence iff the reference substring deleted by either, when aligned, gives identical sequences — for pure homopolymer runs, gap is equivalent iff all bases between min(x,pos+1) and max(x,pos+1)+D-1 are the candidate deleted base (i.e., within the same run).
